strengths: Addresses important gap with first multiview object-level change detection benchmark with 350 diverse video pairs and comprehensive evaluation metrics (per-view, per-scene, per-scene AP_poly)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including detailed ablation studies, systematic failure case analysis (geometry reconstruction, lighting changes, cluttered scenes), and robustness evaluations under varying conditions
Well-designed evaluation protocol with clear per-view tolerance policies and multi-level assessment suitable for different use cases
Training-free method leveraging existing pretrained models (π³, SAM, DINO3) shows pragmatic approach with reasonable generalization potential
Demonstrates practical applicability through robot manipulation use case (cleaning robot) beyond academic benchmarking
Clear presentation with informative visualizations, extensive supplementary materials, and detailed implementation specifications
weaknesses: Method component lacks algorithmic novelty - combines existing techniques (depth reconstruction, feature extraction, region scoring) in straightforward manner without innovative technical contributions
Significant computational efficiency problem: 159.4s per sequence pair vs VLM (30.5s) and CYWS-3D (23.9s) due to SAM mask generation bottleneck; 5-7x slowdown severely limits practical deployment
Persistent performance gaps with high sensitivity to multiple hyperparameters; absolute scores (e.g., 28.9 AP_poly on SD-V) indicate substantial unresolved challenges despite relative improvements

Dataset scale and scope limitations: only 350 video pairs, restricted to indoor environments, limited to small objects, and excludes dynamic objects; reliance on geometry reconstruction limits applicability to sparse/textureless scenes
Heavy dependence on pretrained models (π³, SAM, DINO3) introduces model-specific biases; explicitly acknowledged sensitivity to reconstruction failures prevents reliable deployment

Technical concerns including ad-hoc asymmetric depth handling, per-view evaluation allowing 2 FPs per ground-truth object may be overly lenient, empirically-tuned region merging strategy; reproducibility depends on multiple external dependencies not fully integrated

strengths: Well-designed dataset contribution with object-level annotations across diverse scenes; provides 250 video pairs with 1000+ annotated objects and multiple evaluation subsets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including comparisons against multiple baselines, ablation studies, and testing on additional datasets beyond their own benchmark
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations and failure modes, with detailed analysis of when and why the method fails (Section 7.4)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and grounding in practical robotics applications
Extensive supplementary materials with additional results, implementation details, and edge case analysis
weaknesses: Limited method novelty: The SceneDiff method is essentially a straightforward pipeline combining existing components (π³ depth estimation, SAM segmentation, standard appearance features); lacks genuine technical innovation and relies heavily on pretrained models
Modest experimental results: Per-view AP of 26.9 and per-scene AP of 28.9 on the authors' benchmark is not compelling; performance degrades significantly on more challenging datasets like RC-3D

Significant acknowledged failure modes that are fundamental to the approach: geometry reconstruction failures with limited overlap, cluttered scenes with repetitive items, and strong lighting variations that the method cannot overcome

Dataset limitations for a top-tier venue: Relatively small (250 pairs) with modest object complexity (5-15 objects per frame), mostly constrained to indoor tabletop scenarios with limited geometric diversity compared to modern vision benchmarks

Heavy dependence on pretrained models without principled justification: Method critically relies on π³ for geometry; when reconstruction fails, entire pipeline fails; branding as 'training-free' is misleading given extensive reliance on pretraining

Weak technical contribution in method design: Scoring functions are simple (basic depth/appearance differences), design choices appear ad-hoc with minimal justification for weight selections, instance association uses simplistic cosine similarity

Evaluation metric concerns: Point-based evaluation may not fully capture quality; dynamic threshold determination via maximum entropy (Eq. 13) appears arbitrary; tolerance for replicated predictions seems loose

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Some comparisons may be unfair (e.g., VLM not designed for this task); missing comparisons with recent multi-view reconstruction methods and simpler geometry-free baselines

Reproducibility and scalability issues: While code release promised, implementation details unclear; manual annotation for 250 pairs required substantial effort with no analysis of annotator agreement or scalability

Narrow scope and unclear impact: Problem is specific to indoor scene change detection; broader applicability and downstream impact beyond the demonstrated robot demo unclear; contribution is primarily engineering rather than research innovation

strengths: Novel benchmark addressing an important gap in multiview object change detection with dense, object-level annotations across 350 diverse video pairs and two complementary scene categories
Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation including ablation studies, failure case analysis, challenging scenario exploration, and practical robotic application demonstrations
Effective training-free method that leverages pretrained models for practical deployment while achieving strong empirical results (34-37% relative improvements over baselines)
Practical methodology accommodating both multi-view and two-view scenarios with region-level scoring more suitable for downstream tasks than pixel-level approaches
Thorough documentation with extensive supplementary material providing implementation details, evaluation metrics, annotation tools, and data collection guidelines supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in the proposed method, which primarily combines existing components (π³, DINo, SAM) with standard scoring functions without introducing conceptual innovations
Moderate dataset scale (350 pairs, two scene categories) and scope limited primarily to indoor environments, raising questions about generalization to diverse domains

Evaluation fairness concerns when comparing against methods designed for different tasks (3DGS-CD for novel view synthesis, VLM for text understanding) with some baselines evaluated under suboptimal conditions

Significant acknowledged limitations constraining practical applicability: strong sensitivity to 3D reconstruction quality, degraded performance under lighting variations, inability to detect semantic changes, and challenges with cluttered repetitive scenes
Substantial computational overhead (159.4s per pair) largely from SAM mask generation, slower than several baselines despite training-free design, potentially limiting deployment scenarios
Method entirely dependent on pretrained model quality without any adaptation capability, making it vulnerable to domain shift and unable to benefit from task-specific fine-tuning

strengths: Novel and comprehensive multiview object change detection benchmark with 350 video pairs from 60 diverse scenes and 1,009 densely annotated objects, filling an important gap in existing benchmarks

Thorough experimental validation including ablation studies demonstrating component impact, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and evaluation across four existing datasets beyond the proposed benchmark
Well-motivated technical approach combining geometry reconstruction and semantic features with clear explanation of how 3D alignment disambiguates viewpoint/lighting changes from true scene changes
Strong empirical results showing 53% and 30.8% relative AP improvements over prior work on different benchmarks
Practical demonstration of real-world utility through robot cleaning application showing the method's applicability beyond academic metrics
Comprehensive annotation pipeline with semi-automatic tools and detailed protocols supporting reproducibility and future extensions
Commitment to reproducibility through promised release of dataset, annotation tool, code, and extensive supplementary material with implementation details
Clear presentation with informative visualizations effectively communicating dataset diversity and method pipeline
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of the method—primarily orchestrates existing techniques (π³, SAM, DINO) with straightforward region matching rather than introducing novel algorithms
Training-free design sacrifices end-to-end optimization for generalization, limiting algorithmic contributions and relegating the method to pipeline design

Incomplete treatment of fundamental challenges: geometric reconstruction failures with limited overlap/textureless surfaces and strong lighting variations remain unresolved without novel mitigation strategies
Missing annotation quality metrics such as inter-annotator agreement, which would strengthen confidence in benchmark reliability given acknowledged ambiguity in change definitions
Dataset scale (350 videos from 60 scenes) is modest compared to major vision benchmarks, with most examples concentrated on tabletop/controlled indoor scenarios
Limited baseline comparisons with some using published results rather than re-implementations, and VLM evaluation restricted to a single model
Method assumptions (aligned scene geometry, similar camera trajectories) are implicit but not explicitly stated in limitations section
Computational efficiency not thoroughly analyzed despite sequential dependency on multiple large pretrained models, which could be a practical bottleneck
Generalization beyond tabletop/indoor manipulated scenarios to dynamic outdoor or highly cluttered real-world environments not thoroughly explored

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem of distinguishing real multiview scene changes from viewpoint/illumination artifacts
Provides a comprehensive benchmark (SceneDiff) with 350 video pairs, dense instance-level annotations across 20 scene categories, and thoughtful annotation protocol with SAM2-based tools
Thorough experimental validation including extensive ablation studies, multi-dataset evaluation, sensitivity analysis, and honest discussion of failure modes
Practical real-world application demonstration with robot table tidying task showing tangible utility
Comprehensive supplementary material with implementation details, data collection protocols, and annotation workflows supporting reproducibility
Method thoughtfully combines geometric alignment and appearance matching, with region-level reasoning for handling occlusions and viewpoint variation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: method primarily combines existing pre-trained components (π³ for geometry, DINO for features, SAM for segmentation) without substantive innovation or learning-based fusion

Critical dependence on geometry reconstruction (π³) which fails on sparse scenes, limited overlap, low-texture surfaces, and cluttered environments with repetitive objects—acknowledged in Sec. 7.5 with 11 failure cases
Strong illumination sensitivity significantly degrades performance (Fig. 17), contradicting the claim of handling viewpoint variation robustly across diverse real scenarios

Dataset scale and diversity modest for modern standards: 350 pairs primarily from controlled indoor laboratory settings; limited outdoor/real-world diversity; shorter sequences compared to contemporary benchmarks

Weak comparative validation: two-view change detection (Sec. 5.2) shows minimal improvements (48.0 vs 43.1 AP) despite multiview focus; comparisons with methods not designed for multiview change detection limit conclusions
Numerous hand-tuned hyperparameters and thresholds (λ^geom, λ^feat, τ_cut, τ_merge, τ_occ in Eq. 4) with unclear principled justification or generalization across datasets
Fundamental problem ambiguity acknowledged (Fig. 10) where some scene changes are indistinguishable from pure viewpoint changes, suggesting problem formulation limitations
Method generalization concerns: no investigation of robustness to alternative geometry/feature extractors; performance bounded by frozen pre-trained models' quality

Limited scope relative to venue expectations: contribution is primarily Dataset/Benchmarks with modest algorithmic novelty; for ECCV, algorithmic or theoretical advances are typically expected more heavily than benchmarking
Robot application demonstration limited to single controlled task; computational cost-accuracy tradeoffs not analyzed despite inference times varying from 150ms to >30min across methods

strengths: First comprehensive multiview object change detection benchmark with dense instance-level annotations across 350 video pairs and 20 diverse scene categories
Well-motivated practical problem with clear applications in robotics, warehouse management, and disaster response
Thorough and rigorous experimental validation including ablation studies, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, cross-dataset evaluation, and honest failure case analysis
Sound technical approach that combines geometry and appearance cues effectively, with training-free design enabling good generalization across domains
Excellent presentation quality with clear figures, comprehensive supplementary material, detailed annotation guidelines, and implementation details supporting reproducibility
Demonstrated real-world applicability through closed-loop robotic manipulation experiments
Solid performance improvements over existing methods on multiple benchmarks (53.0-63.5% relative improvement over RC-3D on SceneDiff)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—method is a straightforward pipeline combining existing pretrained models (π³, DINO, SAM) without novel technical contributions
Modest dataset scale (350 video pairs, ~1909 objects) compared to modern computer vision benchmarks; would benefit from larger scale for enabling deep learning approaches
Heavy reliance on pretrained model quality with no means to improve performance without retraining foundation models; fundamentally limited by pose estimation accuracy
Primarily indoor controlled scenes with limited challenging real-world scenarios; underexplored outdoor diversity and complex environments with occlusions
Geometry reconstruction failures acknowledged in sparse overlap and low-texture scenarios, representing a fundamental limitation for the method
Incomplete baseline comparisons with some results sourced from published papers rather than consistent implementations across methods
Modest absolute performance (~60% best case on SceneDiff test set) indicating significant room for improvement; hyperparameter sensitivity with multiple thresholds requiring validation set tuning
Limited systematic error analysis and computational complexity breakdown; generalization to new camera types and domains not thoroughly investigated
Inherent ambiguity in change definition (moved objects vs. removed+added) acknowledged but not thoroughly addressed in evaluation protocol
